GORIOT VS. VAUTRIN: A PROBLEM IN THE RECONSTRUCTION OF LE PÈRE GORIOr S SYSTEM OF VALUES Nilli Diengott Balzac has been accused by his critics of writing immoral works where expe diency, criminality, atheism and materialism are upheld as positive values. Those who do not accuse him of outright immorality charge him with moral ambivalence. As Bellos says, "the critics who attacked the morality of the Comédie humaine cannot be dismissed as simply wrong. Independently of each other, a great number of them 'misread' the novels in the same way, so that one is indeed entitled to speculate on whether Balzac .. . had not in fact created an immoral work by mistake."1 Le Père Goriot is one of the works often mentioned when such charges are made.2 Le Père Goriot substantiates, in my opinion, Bellos' assumption that some thing about the work leads to "misreadings," and it seems clear to me that the ambivalence we feel about the three central characters—Rastignac, Vautrin and Goriot—is responsible for the blurring of the value-system reconstructed by the reader, i.e., the implied author.3 Critics explain the ambivalence in Le Père Goriot in different ways. A biographical explanation is that ambivalence is the result of Balzac's own hesitation between bourgeois conservatism and Romantic anarchism (Savage). Another explanation is that the ambivalence results from the narrator's non-judgmental attitude to his main characters, which blurs the authorial viewpoint (Bellos, Rogers). Other critics attribute it to the characters' contradictory portrayal (Raphael, Hoberg-Petersen) and still others to the inconclusive ending (Bellos, Raphael). It is my purpose to shed new light on the ambivalence of the value-system by bringing forth a new interpretation of the Goriot-Vautrin relationship conveyed through analogies. In a novel narrated by a reliable omniscient narrator who constantly com ments at length on various issues, one might expect such a narrator to be a spokesman for the implied author. However, as critics have noted, large parts of the novel are focalized through Rastignac, and the narrator, though all knowing, is not all-telling.4 Thus, the implied author is not made explicit by the narrator as it is, for instance, in a novel like Middlemarch. 70 All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

Nilli Diengott 71 One means of discovering the implied author5 is the portrayal of the main characters. Two of the central characters, Goriot and Rastignac, seem to repre sent only partially the implied author, i.e., the value-system of the novel. On the one hand Goriot is completely devoted to his daughters and gains the sym pathy of both Rastignac and the reader; at the same time Goriot's paternity is excessive and, but for it, he is "un ouvrier stupide et grossier."6 Rastignac is sympathetically presented because we witness his inner conflict and his pro tection of Goriot, yet throughout the novel Rastignac's moral deterioration, which culminates with his choice at the end of the novel, is criticized. Vau trin, of all the characters, seems to fully represent the implied author. He is presented as a genius, rebel, social philosopher and critic. Even his failures— in convincing Rastignac to follow the course of action he proposes, and his capture by the police—may be considered as strengthening his position as the spokesman for the implied author. The course Rastignac finally chooses is disapproved of by the narrator, and being captured by the police, the repre sentative of the corrupt society constantly attacked by the narrator, is not a real failure. However, as I will show presently, Vautrin is a failure, just like Rastignac and Goriot, and cannot be considered as the spokesman for the implied author because he, too, is ambivalently presented. Thus, an attempt to come to grips with the value-system of the novel is far from being simple. Critics mention Balzac's tendency to view things in polarized terms.7 In deed, in Le Père Goriot as a whole, Rastignac shuttles back and forth between two morally polarized choices. On the one hand success through opportunism, on the other, moral integrity through compassion. At the end of the novel he chooses the former. However, critics ignore a textual element responsible for the blurring of the value-system-the narrator's presentation of Rastignac as facing three choices: "L'Obéissance, la Lutte et la Révolte: la Famille, le Monde et Vautrin" (323). It is my contention that the contradiction between the options the narra tor offers in the above equation and the polarities the novel as a whole pre sents is only apparent. Two of the narrator's terms correspond to Rastignac's two polarized mentors: Vautrin is explicitly associated by the narrator's equa tion with revolt. Goriot, for whom family relations are valued above every thing, is implicitly associated by the same equation with obedience.8 The middle term, "the struggle," which corresponds to the world [of society], is puzzling, since most readers would associate struggle with revolt. And yet the equation presents it as a separate and third choice. A clue to the meaning of this third option can be found in another distinction made by Vautrin between "l'éclat du génie" and "l'adresse de la corruption" (149). Corruption, however, cannot be associated with Goriot-like obedience, since on the one hand it is a means for succeeding and becoming powerful, which Goriot is not, and on the other corruption is reserved for "la médiocrité qui abonde" (150), not for Vautrin, the genius, nor the totally devoted Goriot. It is this third choice that Rasti gnac prefers at the end, rejecting both "stupid obedience" and the "revolt of genius." My explanation of the three-term equation, and especially the middle term (struggle = society = corruption), indicates that Vautrin and Goriot (revolt and obedience) are two options that are antithetical to society. In other words, the novel is polarized, as critics have often claimed, but the polarization is not between Goriot and Vautrin, but rather between society on the one hand and both Goriot and Vautrin on the other. Thus, the narrator's three terms pre sent two poles: opportunism vs. moral integrity and compassion. Goriot's obedience and Vautrin's revolt of genius belong, paradoxically, to the "mor al" pole, which is outside the pale of Paris society, where the road to success is through opportunism and giving up integrity and compassion. Thus, Ras tignac's two rejected mentors, despite their antithetical appearance, are pre sented within the value scheme of the novel as belonging to the same moral pole.9 This apparently strange conclusion is further substantiated by the use of analogies between Goriot and Vautrin. By analogy I mean a pattern "com posed of two fictive components at least (two characters, events, strands of action, etc.) between which there is at least one point of similarity and one of dissimilarity."10 The analogies between Vautrin and Goriot are both explicit and implicit. Goriot explicitly identifies himself with Vautrin when he says he is willing to murder for his daughter and to be imprisoned like Vautrin (308). Most of the analogies, however, are implicit. Goriot is a retired merchant and Vautrin pretends to be one (30). I have already mentioned that both of them fail: Goriot dies alone and poor, while Vautrin is captured by the police. But the most interesting implicit analogies, ignored by critics, form a pattern which associates Goriot, the "Christ de la Paternité" (279), with criminality, while Vautrin, the arch-criminal, is associated with paternity.11 Goriot is suspected by the pension's lodgers of being associated with crime and vice (50), and Rastignac surmises he might be "un voleur ou un receleur" (60), and when he sees him kneading silver Goriot's actions "lui parurent trop criminels" (62). Mme Langeais in describing Goriot's sacrifices for his daughters says that "le père et les enfants ont été complices de ce petit crime" (112). The narrator indicates that Goriot's amassing of wealth during the All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

Nilli Diengott 73 revolution involved some underhanded activities, since he prospered while others starved and kept his wealth well hidden until "il n'y avait plus de dan ger à êtreriche" (125). There is a symmetrical relationship in the analogies between Goriot and Vautrin. In each case a manifest quality is supplemented by an implicit qual ity, which is associated with the apparently antithetical character. Thus, Goriot is a declared father but a covert "criminal," while Vautrin is a declared criminal but a covert "father." The pattern of allusions implying Vautrin's fatherhood is explicitly indicated when Vautrin informs Rastignac that if he is able to escape to America and has no children he intends to leave his fortune to Rastignac, thus indicating that he is an adopting father and Rasti gnac an adopted son (215). In addition, Vautrin refers to himself explicitly as Rastignac's "papa Vautrin" (145, 239). His fatherly feelings for Rastignac can be seen in the manner by which he makes the sleeping Rastignac more comfortable while kissing him and singing to him (240). The analogy between Goriot and Vautrin is further implied by the fact that both characters use women as a means for Rastignac's success—Goriot through Delphine and the apartment he provides for them, Vautrin by having Victorine's brother killed so that Rastignac can marry a rich heiress. Vautrin and Goriot display concern for Rastignac in very similar words: Goriot says, "quelquefois vous aurez besoin de quelqu'un pour vous rendre service, je serai là" (232). And Vautrin, "si tu étais gêné, je t'ai laissé un ami dévoué" (265). In addition, Vautrin tells Rastignac that he knows him "comme si je vous avais fait" (143), i.e., as if he were his own father-creator. The analogies between Goriot and Vautrin discussed above emphasize that Goriot and Vautrin are only apparently antithetical characters, whereas the value-system of the novel implies that they belong to the pole which is the antithesis of the value scheme Rastignac chooses at the end of the novel —corrupt opportunism—a value scheme rejected by the implied author. How ever, the implied author's norms, though apparently capable of being nega tively reconstructed (because we know the values he rejects), are not capable of being positively reconstructed because they are blurred by ambivalence. This ambivalence is indirectly introduced through a heretofore unnoticed analogy between Goriot and Vautrin. A pattern of explicit and implicit reference to both characters suggests that they are tainted. Vautrin's criminality, far from tainting him, is not con demned in the novel, and on the contrary is presented as a magnificent and positive revolt against corrupt society. Yet his desire to become a father is marred by the impossibility of its realization because of the recurrent refer All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

74 Nineteenth-Century French Studies enees, by both Vautrin and the police detective (216, 221, 224, 244), to his homosexuality. Goriot's paternity, which confers upon him a Christ-like status, is presented as tainted by several allusions that suggest that his rela tionship is unnatural, in fact, incestuous. Goriot is suspected by Mme Vauquer of being "un libertin qui avait des goûts étranges" (50), and she finds it natural for him to present his several mistresses as his daughters (52). The narrator seems to confirm her suspicions by asserting that Goriot's snuffbox contained lockets of hair "qui le rendaient en apparence coupable de quelques bonnes fortunes" (41). The daughters are described as living "comme auraient vécu les maltresses d'un vieux seigneur riche" (127) at the expense of their father. Goriot is described as "un amant encore assez jeune pour être heureux d'un stratagème qui le meten commu nication avec sa maltresse" (160), and reacts "dans un violent désespoir de jalousie" (201) at hearing that Rastignac was able to extricate Delphine out of her debts. When Delphine visits him he lies down at her feet "comme en aurait fait l'amant le plus jeune et le plus tendre" (280).12 These allusions are not to be taken literally, but serve as metaphors for indicating that Goriot's paternity is unnatural, in fact, criminal. Thus, the real father but covert crim inal and the real criminal but covert father are both tainted in their paternity. In the value scheme of Le Père Goriot paternity is a crux.13 Goriot, just before his death, shouts angrily, "la patrie périra si les pères sont foulés aux pieds. Cela est clair. La société, le monde roulent sur la paternité, tout croule si les enfants n'aiment pas leurs pères" (342). Society's very foundations stand on the natural relationship between fathers and children. Yet the two father-figures in the novel are failures. Goriot's paternity is perverted and Vau trin's "paternity" is unrealizable. Thus, though the implied author presents the values of society as corrupt, he does not provide within the fictive world of the novel viable alternatives from which Rastignac may choose. The norm of which the implied author approves—represented by natural fatherhood—be longs to a different, lost, or unrealizable world, whereas the norms presented within the fictive world are all tainted or corrupt. The three characters capable of having the "right" values gain our sympathy, consent and identification, yet all fail because none of them possesses the "right" value-system unambiv alently. They are undermined by the implied author whose negative attitude to society is unequivocal but whose positive value-system is left unrealized within the novel. c/o Everyman's University (Israel's Open University) 1 6 Klausner Tel Aviv, Israel 61 392 All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions
